title: Musk Makes the Call: AI5 Chips Go First to Optimus Robots, Tesla Cars Stay on AI4, Which Is Enough for Superhuman Driving
excerpt: Tesla owners still running AI3 asked Musk on X: when will the next-generation AI5 chip make it into cars? The answer was a bit painful—robots first. On November
content_html:
Tesla owners still running AI3 asked Musk on X: when will the next-generation AI5 chip make it into cars? The answer was a bit painful—robots first. On November 22, Musk made it clear when replying to this user: AI5 will be deployed first to Optimus humanoid robots and AI training systems, while cars will remain on AI4, because “AI4 is enough to solve superhuman driving.”

Giving It to Robots First Isn’t Favoritism

This wasn’t a whim: on the Q1 earnings call, Musk already said AI4’s compute was enough to support unsupervised autonomous driving, with safety levels far exceeding human driving, and that the more advanced AI5 should be fed first to Optimus and the company’s AI training clusters. Tech outlet Teslarati believes Tesla’s strategic focus is shifting toward embodied intelligence: humanoid robots must simultaneously handle environmental perception, path planning, multi-degree-of-freedom motion control, and real-time interaction, placing more complex demands on compute, memory, and energy efficiency than cars.

AI5 Has Taped Out, Mass Production in 2027

AI5 has taped out and entered trial production, with mass production set for 2027. Its compute is about 12 times that of AI4, and its memory is planned at about 96GB—three times the roughly 32GB of the current AI4. Larger memory can run more complex AI models, at the cost of rising costs, power consumption, and thermal pressure. As for the current AI4 (also called HW4), it relies on two custom SoCs to form the in-car autonomous driving compute platform, each containing 3 neural network accelerators called TRIP, for 6 in total. Paired with GDDR6 memory, it handles real-time tasks such as camera image understanding, path planning, and vehicle control. In Musk’s view, this setup is enough for driving; it’s robots that truly need more compute.
